title: Crypto Money Still Matters for the Midterms
summary: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.The crypto industry has always moved in cycles: booms and busts; bull markets and harsh, unforgiving “w...
content:
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.

The crypto industry has always moved in cycles: booms and busts; bull markets and harsh, unforgiving “winters.” We’re in something of a lull right now: Bitcoin, the original cryptocurrency, is worth about two-thirds of what it was last fall. Meanwhile, investors are turning their attention to flashier innovations in artificial intelligence. About half of Americans now use AI chatbots, whereas just about a fifth of the country has ever used or invested in crypto.

But the crypto industry isn’t dead—as of today, the combined value of all digital currencies is still more than $2.7 trillion—and neither are its political ambitions. Crypto companies have so far put $206 million toward this year’s midterm elections, more than any other corporate sector, including the AI industry, according to a Public Citizen analysis of OpenSecrets and Federal Election Commission data. Fairshake, the industry’s foremost super PAC, has a giant war chest and a reputation for backing winners from both parties (Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has reportedly warned of the risks of crossing it). Crypto is much further from the spotlight now than it was during its 2024 election-spending spree; back then, the industry was flush with cash, but its reputation was still recovering from the crash of two years prior and from the spectacle of Sam Bankman-Fried’s fraud trial. Even as Americans continue to distrust crypto, they’re now reserving their outrage for other corners of the tech industry, such as data centers and surveillance cameras. Although crypto is no longer as central to the public conversation, it’s still finding ways to flex its power.

Fairshake first established itself as a major force during the 2024 election cycle, spending about $133 million in support of its chosen candidates. It started 2026 with a reported $193 million in the bank and has so far spent close to $70 million elevating politicians with an industry-friendly agenda. Fairshake’s record this year has been incredibly strong. Despite a few fairly significant losses, 50 of the 54 candidates it backed ended up winning their race. Not all of them won entirely because of Fairshake’s intervention: Some were incumbents who didn’t have a serious challenger. But an endorsement from Fairshake and its affiliate PACs tends to come with major financial support. The group spent more than $12 million to get a pro-crypto Republican into the general election for Alabama’s open Senate seat—it was “by far the biggest spender” in the primary, per The New York Times. And Protect Progress, Fairshake’s Democrat-focused PAC, spent more than $5 million to make another pro-crypto politician the party’s nominee for the House in Maryland’s Fifth District.

Some candidates have incorporated these extreme interventions into their campaign strategy, accusing crypto-backed opponents of being in the industry’s pocket. Minnesota’s Peggy Flanagan, who won the state’s Democratic primary for the Senate, bashed her opponent for being pro-crypto and for being “funded by crypto and AIPAC and health-insurance companies.” In Florida’s Twenty-Fourth District, Fairshake spent more than $2 million trying to defeat Oliver Gilbert’s bid for the House, but Gilbert won his primary anyway. “Trump and his crypto con-artist billionaires just put a target on my back,” he said in one ad. Bloomberg reports that political candidates have purchased more ads mentioning the word crypto this year than they have in any of the past five years, and that the majority of these candidates are anti-crypto.

Voters have never been all that passionate about crypto, and the Americans who do care about the tech are still disinclined to trust it. But the country’s attention has been elsewhere lately. Three-quarters of Americans say they’d oppose the construction of a data center in their community. Local governments across the country are now canceling contracts for Flock’s AI-enabled license-plate readers over rising fears of improper surveillance. In a bipartisan effort, 47 states, plus Washington, D.C., and U.S. territories, recently took Meta to trial for allegedly damaging “the mental and physical wellbeing of America’s youth” with its social-media platforms (the company just settled and will pay up to $17.1 billion). Although Fairshake’s spending spree has drawn attention to the role of crypto in politics, there’s been no equivalent public movement this year against the sector. When Politico asked Cynthia Lummis, arguably the country’s most pro-crypto senator, whether voters care about crypto, she replied, “No.”

To get a sense of how much the industry’s public profile has shifted, it’s useful to think back on the past six years. Permit me a short history lesson.

During the coronavirus pandemic, a speculative bubble massively boosted the industry’s profile. Then, in 2022, everything melted down. Bitcoin lost more than 60 percent of its value, and a series of high-profile corporate implosions created chaos throughout the sector. Executives from several major crypto companies were charged with fraud, but it was FTX’s Bankman-Fried who became, at least for a while, the industry’s criminal mascot. Last year, crypto ended up with a new mascot in the form of Donald Trump. Once in office, he threw his support behind the industry, implementing a deregulatory agenda and signing a major crypto bill into law. As cryptocurrencies soared, he also personally made $1.4 billion from his family’s businesses in the sector, leading to widespread allegations of corruption.

As digital currencies have come back down to earth, they have started to feel more mundane. Crypto persists in partnerships with major financial institutions, in exchange-trading funds, and in the payment apps you may already have on your phone. None of this is particularly exciting—we’re unlikely to see an NFT at the Met Gala next year, as we did in 2021, or at the upcoming MTV Video Music Awards, as we did in 2022—yet it’s still a massive industry. Without that same level of visibility, crypto interests aren’t necessarily a public “target the way they were with the fallout of FTX, but on the other hand, they’ve had to struggle to stay relevant,” Mark Hays, an associate director at Americans for Financial Reform (a crypto-critical watchdog), told me; one of their strategies is to “continue to spend heavily to show that they still have clout.” The industry has plenty of battles left to fight, though—and plenty of cash to put toward winning them.

Evening Read

Illustration by Cecilia Reeve

The Missing Ingredient of Modern Life

By Ian Bogost

You have, by now, probably come across the notion of maxxing—looks-maxxing, sleep-maxxing, protein-maxxing, potassium-maxxing, sun-maxxing, testosterone-maxxing. Etymologically speaking, maxxing seems to be a descendant of somewhat recent slang—for those of us who remember the late 20th century, “maxin’ and relaxin’ ” and “to the max” both come to mind—but in practice, maxxing is a reductionist worldview cloaked in expansionist language.

The term is often invoked to describe a narrowly focused goal: If you’re maxxing, you’re likely trying to make yourself smaller, sharper, more chiseled. Maxxing requires sacrifice. It requires careful measurement. And in this way, maxxing is a consequence of our broader optimization-obsessed culture, a fixation fueled by every product, device, app, and service that trains people to collect and analyze data generated by their own behavior.

title: There’s No Such Thing as an AI ‘Lab’
summary: When did AI companies become AI labs? That term, and the image of studious, exacting white-coated scientists that it conjures, has become curiously entrenched as a descriptor for the businesses swiftly escorting the world into an existentially unsettling future. AI companies themselves have embraced...
content:
When did AI companies become AI labs? That term, and the image of studious, exacting white-coated scientists that it conjures, has become curiously entrenched as a descriptor for the businesses swiftly escorting the world into an existentially unsettling future. AI companies themselves have embraced the label: When Chris Olah, a co-founder of Anthropic, addressed the pope earlier this year, he repeatedly referred to his company, one of the most powerful AI enterprises in the world, as a lab. Industry press releases, technology commentators, and news publications have all picked up the word too. You’ll see the term on transit advertisements in San Francisco and in the pages of The New York Times (and, yes, The Atlantic).

Here is my proposal: Everyone, please stop. This term has gone too far. Although AI companies do invest heavily in research and development, using a word typically associated with groups of truth-seeking scientists is misleading, odd, and too favorable to these companies’ own ends. As a software engineer working in tech, I’ve seen little evidence that AI companies’ research practices differ significantly from those of the rest of the tech industry. Google and Microsoft, for example, have robust research divisions, but we still call them companies. So why has the laboratory term become so deeply enmeshed with AI?

Part of the reason is historical. Over the past century, research laboratories have played a crucial role in computer science. Studies performed at Bell Labs, one of America’s first industrial labs, resulted in the development of the transistor and the cellular network. In the 1970s, scientists at the MIT Laboratory for Computer Science pioneered the foundations of modern cryptography. As the Harvard historian Steven Shapin writes in his book The Scientific Life, countless innovations such as these that originated in corporate labs during the 20th century helped change the public’s perception of science. No longer simply knowledge for knowledge’s sake, science became viewed as a key engine of societal and economic progress.

In their early years, OpenAI and Anthropic mainly performed research, similar to other industrial labs. Since then, however, they have commercialized rapidly: Each company is now valued near $1 trillion and generates billions in quarterly revenue. Holding on to the lab label seems to have the obvious PR benefit of allowing both companies to lean into their scientific legacy. Because of concerns about child safety, privacy, and job displacement, Americans largely hold a negative perception of the industry—and tech as a whole. That’s translated into popular opposition from politicians, data-center activists, and religious leaders who are concerned about the outsize influence of these companies: Spending on AI as a share of U.S. GDP now rivals defense spending. Meanwhile, scientists remain relatively popular. A 2026 Pew Research Center poll found that more than 75 percent of Americans trust scientists to act in the public interest, but the majority do not trust business leaders to do the same. These positive connotations associated with scientific research help the AI industry signal altruism while downplaying their profit-making ambitions. OpenAI and Anthropic’s leaders write at length about how AI’s risks and perils must be carefully studied for the sake of humanity. Research is portrayed as essential to this mission: OpenAI says it treats “safety as a science,” and Anthropic writes that “providing trustworthy research” will improve policy outcomes.

The problem is, these companies act much more like private enterprises than bastions of science. Much of the research listed in the Publications section on both Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s websites are not peer-reviewed papers accepted by scholarly outlets. I examined 100 recent pieces of research from both companies’ Research pages; the overwhelming majority had no corresponding peer-reviewed paper accepted by a conference or journal. It’s unclear whether these were submitted to academic venues and, if so, whether they were rejected, are under review, or are forthcoming. (Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic responded to requests for comment.)

Legal risks and long peer-review cycles are typically cited as reasons that fast-moving tech companies seldom share data or engage in peer review. And to its credit, the industry doesn’t always choose research topics that paint its products in a positive light. Anthropic has conducted studies on its models’ undesirable behaviors, such as disempowerment and sycophancy.

Even so, Anthropic has a habit of landing on ambiguity about the fallout of its technology. In its education report, for instance, Anthropic, the entity best equipped to observe whether students are using Claude to cheat, concludes that the question of “How much are students using AI to cheat?” is “hard to answer.”

The practice of assuming scientific authority while exercising potentially biased research practices has more in common with quasi-scientific advocacy organizations than it does with traditional laboratories. Take, for example, the George C. Marshall Institute, a think tank founded in 1984 whose leaders worked closely with the Reagan White House. The institute, whose publications defended oil interests and the tobacco industry, operated under the motto “Science for better public policy.” As the historians Naomi Oreskes and Erik Conway reported in the book Merchants of Doubt, the institute strategically refused to publish in journals subject to independent peer review. Instead, it disseminated reports and briefings to policy makers that merely reproduced the “trappings of scientific argumentation—graphs, charts, references, and the like.”

If Anthropic, OpenAI, and other AI giants want to keep referring to themselves as labs, they should adhere to scientific best practices: open-sourcing code, preregistering studies, and, most important, subjecting research to independent peer review. Ultimately, AI companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI aren’t tweedy labs doing arcane research—they’re industry-defining corporations reshaping our workplaces, our schools, and our communities. Holding them accountable could start with calling them out for what they are—and what they aren’t.

title: What Tech Titans Don’t Understand About Sci-Fi
summary: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books. Sign up for it here.When I read Thomas More’s Utopia in college, the main thing I retained was that the inhabitants of More’s imaginary island worked just six hours a day and earned what we might now call a uni...
content:
This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books. Sign up for it here.

When I read Thomas More’s Utopia in college, the main thing I retained was that the inhabitants of More’s imaginary island worked just six hours a day and earned what we might now call a universal basic income. But the fact that I came away from this 16th-century classic with only visions of a shorter workday and a generous allowance says more about my undergraduate habits than it does about More’s ideas or intentions. Looking back recently, I remembered that his civilization wasn’t exactly the campus commune of my dreams. Its citizens held slaves, some of whom were shackled for committing adultery. The punishment for premarital sex, meanwhile, was permanent celibacy; the whole place sounded like a punitive surveillance state. I’d somehow missed all of this initially. Still, as Gal Beckerman noted this week in an Atlantic essay about Silicon Valley’s misreadings of science fiction, I wasn’t the first person to make this type of error. Fortunately, my myopia was harmless. Not all misunderstandings are.

First, here are five new stories from The Atlantic Books Section:

  • The sexual politics of the “bed trick”
  • What Howard Zinn got wrong
  • “Red Death,” a poem by Dorothea Lasky
  • What to read to wake up your brain
  • Roy Cohn did it first.

In her new book, The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State, the historian Jill Lepore close-reads the science-fiction books that proved formative for Elon Musk, Sam Altman, and Peter Thiel. In their early-teen years, these future billionaires devoured the works of Robert Heinlein, Isaac Asimov, Arthur C. Clarke, and other dark fantasists—but they seem to still hold on to the blinkered interpretations from their youth. Their collective misunderstandings fascinated Beckerman. “What they seemed not to get,” he writes of these men, “was that these were cautionary tales, stories that projected deep societal worries into space or onto a future many millennia away.” Instead of seeing the dysfunction behind these invented societies, “these boys just thought the killer robots sounded cool.” Lepore argues that these seeming misreads are partly responsible for their obsessions with technological progress—no matter the human cost.

Three centuries after More coined the word utopia (which sounds in Greek like “good place” but actually means “no place”), the philosopher John Stuart Mill effectively popularized its opposite, dystopia, to describe worlds in which the worst things come to pass. In the 20th century, dystopia became a key feature of science fiction. Some of my favorite works in the genre introduce us to societies that seem idyllic, before revealing the rot within these supposedly perfect worlds. They aim, I think, to show that any utopia is probably too good to be true. It’s no place—or worse.

More’s Utopia isn’t all that different; it depicts a society that readers might not actually want to live in. More, an English Catholic leader who was executed by King Henry VIII, probably didn’t mean to advocate for an essentially communist society with legalized euthanasia. Critics have long speculated that his depiction was satirical—that the first utopian literary work was, at least in part, dystopian. This wouldn’t surprise me, because years of living and reading have conditioned me to accept that every paradise has a dark side.

This is why I was dismayed to hear Sam Altman say, earlier this year, that an AI-driven process to choose the U.S. president could be “awesome.” Seventy years ago, in his short story “Franchise,” Asimov imagined one variation on this scenario: A computer picks one median American to “vote” for president. In the story, democracy becomes nothing more than a statistical quirk. At a moment when artificial intelligence threatens to change society irrevocably, I have to agree with Beckerman: “What happens next,” he writes, “may depend on whether these boys grow up and finally recognize what they failed to see before.”

Illustration by Matteo Giuseppe Pani / The Atlantic*

We Are Living in the Fantasy World of 13-Year-Old Boys

By Gal Beckerman

Many of the tech billionaires who built our world have taken the wrong lessons from their favorite science fiction.

Read the full article.

What to Read

Providence, by Max Barry

Seven years before the start of this novel, an alien species slaughtered everyone aboard a human spaceship—Earth’s first contact with extraterrestrials. Providence follows the four-person crew of an interstellar warship on a multiyear mission of revenge. Through each voyager’s distinct perspective, the book explores artificial intelligence, social media, and the effects of extended isolation. One character doesn’t care about these aliens’ civilization; he is content just to kill as many as possible. Another is driven to discover more; a third is focused on maintaining the morale of the others, even as she herself unravels. And their captain has to balance their individual needs against the requirements of the mission. Barry provides riveting, rewarding action without sacrificing smarts or character development. This quick read explores mankind’s dueling urges to connect and destroy, our divergent responses to the unknown, and how far some among us will go to protect ourselves and the people we care about.

From our list: Six books that take you to space

Out Next Week

📚 All The Presidents’ Wars, by Peter Bergen

📚 Everyman: The Untold Story of Economics, by Antara Haldar

📚 Medea: A Life, by Edith Hall

Your Weekend Read

Erica Hernandez

Woodstock, Lilith Fair, and Taco Bell Rolled Into One

By Spencer Kornhaber

Eli is a campy artist of questionable earnestness, but her statement was in line with the mood of Daisy Chain—a place where girlish aesthetics that are so often seen as frivolous could accompany calls for revolution. Organized by the 23-year-old pop star Olivia Rodrigo, the inaugural edition of the festival featured an all-female lineup and raised $20 million—half of which was donated by Melinda French Gates—for an array of women’s-rights organizations, including Planned Parenthood and the National Domestic Workers Alliance. Even as a brutal heat wave threatened to smother the energy, the fest felt like a cheerful coming-out party—an announcement of the political commitments of a generation of mainstream artists more famous for singing about the self than about society.

title: The Meaning of the Lindsay Clancy Mistrial
summary: During the five weeks of her murder trial, Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of murdering her three young children in 2023, spoke barely a word. She has been on display for the entirety of her livestreamed trial, sitting in her wheelchair beside her lawyer at the defense table. At one...
content:
During the five weeks of her murder trial, Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of murdering her three young children in 2023, spoke barely a word. She has been on display for the entirety of her livestreamed trial, sitting in her wheelchair beside her lawyer at the defense table. At one point, when the prosecution walked the jury through the children’s autopsy reports, she hunched over, racked with sobs, crying out, “I can’t do this!” But mostly, Clancy has remained silent and wide-eyed, her gaze wandering around the courtroom as though searching for something.

The judge in the case has just declared a mistrial because the jury has been unable to reach a unanimous verdict. But the viewing public, in the absence of Clancy’s own explanation of her experiences leading up to and after the killings, has projected its own ideas onto the case and rendered its own verdict. Some people have interpreted Clancy’s trial as a referendum on women’s postpartum mental health. Others have developed elaborate conspiracy theories maintaining that Clancy’s ex-husband, Patrick, is actually the guilty party. Still others have construed Clancy’s story as evidence for their own niche political beliefs.

These are all comforting narratives, in some sense, because they imply an underlying logic that imbues the events with meaning and provides a road map for catharsis. Yet the jury’s inability to arrive at a verdict makes plain that a careful evaluation of the facts does not yield an easily intelligible conclusion. The reality may be darker and more despairing: that something so dramatic and destructive could, in the end, mean nothing at all.

As Clancy’s trial has progressed, dozens of women wearing pink have appeared at organized rallies outside the courthouse in Plymouth, Massachusetts, holding signs signaling a kind of support for her. “Any one of us who have dealt with mental health, anxiety, depression, postpartum—I think we just know that any one of us could be sitting in her chair,” the organizer of a recent event billed as an opportunity to “stand in peace for Lindsay” told a local news outlet.

There is something inherently unsettling about any public expression of support for a confessed killer, but these gatherings and their associated social-media movements have not seemed aimed at improving Clancy’s odds of success in court. Instead, these demonstrations suggest that Clancy has for some women become a symbolic figure: the devoted but suffering mother martyred by the relentless, punishing demands of her children’s early years and left to suffer by a flawed and fractured health-care system. Many women have felt overwhelmed to the point of drowning in the months after giving birth, and many have sought help but failed to receive it. Clancy’s case, in her supporters’ imagination, appears to be the sum of all those biological and social hazards. What happened to Clancy, in this view, was predictable, and thus preventable.

[Stephanie McCrummen: The women who are obsessed with Lindsay Clancy]

That’s a tidy narrative about what took place in Duxbury that night in 2023, when Clancy strangled her three young children to death, then attempted to end her own life by swallowing prescription drugs, slashing her neck and wrists, and then jumping out of a window. A possible upshot of this view is that it may raise awareness about the inadequacy of treatment options for postpartum mental illnesses—to the degree that raising awareness about any given issue ever meaningfully changes anything. And some elements of it seem inarguably true, such as the idea that Clancy’s psychiatric care was woefully uncoordinated. But this theory also has the odd effect of making Clancy the star of her own murder trial, for whom the viewer at home may be encouraged to root, which risks eliding the gravity of what she did.

Simultaneously believing that someone is relatable and vulnerable and that they are nevertheless guilty of and accountable for heinous crimes is, however, cognitively tricky. I suspect that that tension is the origin of a similarly enormous groundswell of conspiracy theorizing about Clancy’s case that has pervaded social media. Although those theories vary, they generally maintain that Clancy is factually innocent of the killings and that her ex-husband is instead guilty of murdering the children, attempting to murder Clancy, and framing his ex-wife for the deaths. Proponents typically cite as proof any number of purported facts presented at trial, such as that Clancy’s fingerprints weren’t found on the exercise bands used to strangle the children, or that her core body temperature upon her arrival to the hospital called the prosecution’s timeline of events into question. Clancy is, in these tellings, a victim of spousal abuse akin to torture, whose partner cruelly exploited her postpartum suffering in order to dispose of his family.

That, too, is a tidy story with symbolic significance: For those who deny her guilt, Clancy’s life and fate become a nightmare of female subjugation. This view morphs a reasonable claim that Patrick ought to have been more attentive to Clancy’s deteriorating mental state into a much stronger insistence that he is in fact fully culpable for what happened, having carefully plotted the entire sequence of events. Clancy’s story, then, becomes a parable about male violence against women.

Yet this embrace of Clancy as the true victim of her crimes has triggered an online backlash on the political right that maintains that liberal-female support for Clancy is a naked expression of latent female tendencies toward violence against children and an indication that liberal women are unstable and dangerous. (This despite the fact that women actually have varying views on the case, and that men kill the majority of children murdered in the United States.) That thinking also mistakenly takes Clancy to be a representative Everywoman, this time standing in for the threatening volatility of liberal women writ large.

[Elizabeth Bruenig: Why Lindsay Clancy’s insanity defense might fail]

All of these views of Clancy’s case strive to make sense of her alleged crimes: This trial must mean that mothers in America are crucially underserved, or that men in America are chauvinistically exploitative, or that women in America are secretly a danger to themselves and others. Some of those readings are more compelling than others, but they all seem to overemphasize what is generalizable about the case while understating what is unique, particular, and hyper-specific about what happened. The broader the statements about this case are, the less they have to do with the events as they really occurred.

Clancy’s experience was inarguably extreme. If, as the defense claims, she was suffering from postpartum psychosis, it was an ultra-rare expression of an already uncommon condition. Her psychiatric care was, per a subsequent malpractice lawsuit, allegedly mismanaged, and the severity of her purported adverse reactions to widely used medications was highly unusual. She was undoubtedly suffering in the months leading up to the murders, and it’s possible that the right degree of support could have prevented what happened, but it’s likewise true that nobody could have reasonably predicted what happened. More than any general theme or idea, Clancy’s crimes seem to have hinged on a moment of catastrophic dysfunction. Life, in the end, defies a great deal of neat storytelling.

For the past several weeks, Clancy’s case has been heard in the court of public opinion. At this point, people seem desperate for answers about why these deaths happened and what they mean, or at least a guarantee that something we’ve learned from this case will prevent similar tragedies from happening in the future. Many such onlookers have hoped that the trial verdict will supply such insights. This hope now appears to have been in vain.

Prosecutors in Clancy’s case must now decide whether to retry her, negotiate a plea deal, or drop the charges altogether. No matter what they choose, this case will continue to frustrate those trying to make sense of it.

Clancy herself, with her haunted, bewildered gaze, seems to already understand what her well-meaning supporters and their opponents can’t yet come to terms with: There is no making sense of what happened, and no greater wisdom to learn from it. At the core of all of this is a void, and nothing emanates from it but the assurance of everlasting pain.

title: OpenAI Wants to Talk About The Federalist Papers
summary: Late last month, OpenAI launched a rather grand mission: nothing less than defending individual political freedom in an age of all-powerful machines. The company’s “Strategic Futures” team has styled itself, in a sense, as inheriting the task of America’s Founding Fathers: “We labor in service of th...
content:
Late last month, OpenAI launched a rather grand mission: nothing less than defending individual political freedom in an age of all-powerful machines. The company’s “Strategic Futures” team has styled itself, in a sense, as inheriting the task of America’s Founding Fathers: “We labor in service of the ideals of free expression and individual liberty that are enshrined in the humble parchment of the U.S. Constitution,” Dean Ball, the team’s leader, wrote in a new OpenAI blog post. (The post opens with a quote from James Madison in The Federalist Papers.)

Ball worries that advanced AI could radically concentrate power in the hands of those who control it, displacing labor in ways that disempower humans. In an extreme scenario, governments will have no need to listen to their citizens if there are robots to wage wars and omniscient software to run the bureaucracy. Ball is interested in studying what new political institutions might be needed to avoid this fate.

Many Americans—a majority of whom express distrust toward the AI industry, outrage about data centers, and fears about their job security—already seem to be feeling this loss of agency very deeply. And the AI boom has already generated enormous amounts of wealth in just a handful of tech companies—including OpenAI itself. To say the least, it’s paradoxical for one of the most influential companies in the world’s most powerful industry to decry the AI-enabled concentration of power. So I reached out to Ball to understand more about his unease about the industry he works in, and how he wants to see the United States adapt to AI.

Ball, who studies AI policy, is something of a minor celebrity in the industry. Last year, he joined the White House as an AI adviser and helped write the Trump administration’s AI Action Plan, a policy road map for the technology. He eventually departed, seemingly on good terms, from the administration before publicly lambasting it during its dispute with Anthropic earlier this year. Then, in July, he joined OpenAI. “My view is that we basically have transformative AI in the world now,” Ball told me. “You’re living in a world that is being transformed. It is happening.”

This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Matteo Wong: You write that concentration of power through AI could upend the basic human freedoms enshrined in the U.S. Constitution. Can you elaborate on how?

Dean Ball: Fundamentally, political power is the geographically bounded ability to wield the monopoly on legitimate force and violence. Doing so has heretofore required the cooperation of a great many human beings. You needed militaries, you needed people in those militaries, and you needed people to keep those militaries fed and supplied. And you needed people to pay for all of that through taxation. So people had a seat at the table because, in some sense, everything is being provided by them.

Now you have to assume that robotics is going to advance soon in the same way that general digital intelligence has. Maybe it will take longer than I think. But at that point, the ability to project violence no longer requires people. And it is also conceivable that AI might generate sufficient revenue that the government would not need to rely on taxing people.

If you look at the politics of AI, I think Americans are smart and have a sense that their seat at the table might be getting smaller. They’re right to be scared.

Wong: You’re talking about concentration of power in the government, but generative AI is a technology developed in the private sector. There is potential for a rare and even unprecedented concentration of power in industry. What risks does that pose?

Ball: You’re not trying to avoid all concentration of power, but to balance it. If this era gives rise to corporations that have a tremendous amount of power in the world, I think that’s good—so long as those organizations are governed. In other words, so long as the government that oversees them grows in lockstep.

People tend to assume that AI residing in private hands is inherently a concentration-of-power risk. But I think that an extremely well-run, government-owned superintelligence lab is a bigger concentration-of-power risk than a polycentric world where there are many superintelligences made by different, competing companies overseen by a government. Monopolies are the concern.

Wong: As far as private concentration of power goes, there are arguably now two frontier labs, your employer and Anthropic. The market doesn’t seem to be providing many checks on them.

Ball: I think it’s a fiercely competitive market right now. And China, of course, is delivering highly capable open-source models. It’s possible this is going to commodify the products that OpenAI and Anthropic offer. I don’t agree with that, but you can’t dismiss it as a crazy outcome. OpenAI’s mission is to deliver artificial general intelligence safely to the world. If that means we’re more like a utility than we are like a big, fancy tech company, so be it.

Wong: This brings us to the core of your essay. If today’s political institutions and market dynamics are not up to the task of protecting human freedom during an AI era, what must change?

Ball: There are AI regulations that I think are sensible to pass. States have passed hundreds of laws about artificial intelligence, and those things are not satisfying the demands of people. What we will need is new political institutions that give us a way of talking about the rate of acceleration in our society.

I’m imagining a federal body could dictate the ratio that an AI lab is allowed to spend on internal deployment of models to do automated AI research. You could say that, this month, you’re going to be allowed to use 45 percent of your compute for that, and next month, it’ll be 47 percent or 52 percent or some other number. That might slow the rate of AI development, but then a company could use that extra compute to lower costs for consumers. Then this dial for AI development would also become a mechanism with the dual effect of slowing or increasing the rate of technological diffusion.

The closest structural analogy that we have is probably interest rates, which is a kind of hyper-parameter on the economy that policy makers can tune. The Federal Reserve is an institution in and of itself, and on top of that, there is an enormous apparatus that exists, including a bond market, interest-rate traders, analysts, media commentary, political oversight in the form of Congress. All of that taken together, in my view, would constitute the institutional complex. That’s a type of political institution. I’m not saying we need to create a new branch of government or something.

Wong: That makes sense regarding the pace of development and diffusion. I’m not totally following how such a measure ties back to your concerns about human freedoms.

Ball: It’s one example of an institution that would give people a sense of meaningful political control over the technology. However, I do not think that the optimal outcome is one in which we take a vote on every single aspect of technological change. I’m not really a fan of data-center moratoria, but I understand that the American public is pulling a lever, and they think it is the one lever they have.

Wong: What role can OpenAI, Anthropic, and the rest of the industry play in trying to imagine these institutions and bring them into existence?

Ball: I think the AI industry has actually been pretty good stewards, all things considered. No surprise that I’m saying this, because I’m from the AI industry, but there’s a reason that I am working in it. I would not say that every frontier AI company always has performed at 100 percent, by no means. But in the future, we may approach points where more costly things have to occur. The AI industry might have to do things that are not in its interest.

Wong: Does your research agenda extend to economic freedoms—that is, how AI could affect the economy and distribution of wealth?

Ball: The main thing we know how to do on that front is to invest in technological innovation and try to grow the economy by making new things possible.

Wong: I think a lot of people would look at past products and technologies that have come out of Silicon Valley and think that what those enabled was a tremendous concentration of wealth and influence in a small number of companies—

Ball: I’m not going to grant you that characterization of Silicon Valley. Has everything been perfect? Absolutely not. But my goodness, people have access to tremendous riches of information now; you can cause food to appear at your doorstep, which would have seemed like magic to the vast majority of humans who have ever lived.

Wong: I could also point to the gig economy and the economics of Amazon and argue that those have not been good for a lot of people, including those who labor to make all that “magic” happen. It’s not magic.

Ball: No one’s saying it’s magic. I’m saying it’s hard work. I was getting gas in rural Virginia recently, and when a woman came in wearing an Amazon vest, everyone congratulated her on the big new job. She was proud, and I don’t think we should belittle people for that.

And by the way, people like you, Matteo—not to demonize you—will speak out of both sides of your mouth on this. On the one hand, you’ll talk about how the gig economy is dehumanizing, and blah blah blah. But then the second anyone tries to introduce any autonomy into that and have, say, drone deliveries instead of people biking all around cities delivering meals, you’ll say, My God, you’re taking away the work from this gig economy.

I’m less than thrilled by our current world, like everyone. But the existence of wealth is good. Innovators capture a shockingly small amount of the value that they create in society. If OpenAI is a fantastically successful company 10 years from now, a generational company, my bet is that we will capture a single-digit fraction of the value that AGI creates in this world. Wealth is not some resource that we divide up; it’s something we create. That’s the magic.

Wong: But wealth is also something that’s divided up. One could alternatively look at generative AI and think of it as a particularly wealth-concentrating technology. To ask again, is wealth distribution something your team is thinking about?

Ball: I don’t think we should invent a solution in search of a problem. So we shouldn’t invent some elaborate mechanism of wealth redistribution if today’s tax system works out. But we also have to prepare for a world in which that isn’t true.

title: UN votes to adopt new world map that shows Africa’s true scale

content:
Togo-sponsored resolution called to phase out traditional map that depicts continent as similar size to Greenland

The United Nations has voted to adopt a resolution for the world to formally phase out the traditional Mercator map of the globe in favour of one that more accurately displays Africa’s size.

In a session at its headquarters in New York, the UN general assembly officially retired the 16th-century Mercator projection in favour of one based on the more accurate 2018 Equal Earth design.

Pedro Sánchez continues to defend Rabat after police report claiming border forces helped 70,000 cross border

  • Europe live – latest updates

Spain has seen no evidence “whatsoever” that Morocco planned or facilitated a mass border breach into its north African territory of Ceuta, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has told parliament.

The address on Thursday followed the emergence of a police report, commissioned by a judge and widely quoted in the media, claiming Moroccan border forces had actively aided about 70,000 people to cross the border in late July.

content:
Claim relating to 1960 attack on hundreds of protesters part of wave of litigation over apartheid crimes in South Africa

The day dawned brightly on 21 March 1960, as residents of the South African township of Sharpeville gathered to protest against pass laws, which forced “Black, Indian and Coloured” South Africans to carry documents at all times specifying where they were allowed to be.

Abraham Mofokeng joined the march, one of dozens organised nationwide by the Pan Africanist Congress (PAC), a breakaway group from the African National Congress (ANC). “The weather was very nice, the sun was out. You could not have suspected that the day would go so horribly,” said Mofokeng, who was then a 20-year-old factory worker.

Referendum result means fewer seats in parliament and new rules on candidates, ahead of December elections

Guinea-Bissau voters have approved a new constitution, which critics say will undermine democracy, that significantly expands presidential powers ahead of elections due in December.

According to provisional results, 70% of voters approved sweeping changes in the tiny west African state’s first constitutional amendment since revisions that ended the one-party socialist state more than three decades ago.

content:
Study reveals that pesticide poisoning kills 11,000 people each year, with India accounting for nearly 60% of fatalities

Almost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every single year, a study has found.

Using publicly available data from 2006-2023, the study, which was commissioned by Pesticide Action Network, found there to be an estimated 402-433m cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning of farmers and farm workers every year.
